analysis.one_liner: Bars meatpackers from buying cattle and hogs under opaque formula-priced contracts, requiring firm prices and open bidding instead.
analysis.headline: The bill died in the Senate Agriculture Committee without a hearing, a vote, or a single cosponsor.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would change the Packers and Stockyards Act, a 1921 law that governs how livestock is bought and sold, to restrict the forward contracts meatpackers use to buy cattle and hogs. Under it, a packer could not use a contract whose price is set later by a formula, could not use a contract without a firm dollar price set on the day the deal is made, would have to offer contracts through open bidding that sellers can watch, and could not use a single contract to lock up more than 40 cattle or 30 hogs [S2] [S3]. The goal is to make pricing between ranchers and the big meat companies more open and competitive [S2].
analysis.who_benefits: Cattle ranchers and hog farmers who sell to meatpackers would gain if the bill passed. They would know the price when they sign a delivery contract instead of being paid later by a formula, they could see competing bids instead of accepting one take-it-or-leave-it offer, and small sellers would be protected from contracts that sweep up more than 40 cattle or 30 hogs at once [S2] [S3]. Consumers who depend on competitive livestock markets also have a stake, since concentrated buying power at the packer level can depress the prices that flow back through the food chain [S2].

how_it_helps.text: Contracts would have to carry a firm base price equal to a fixed dollar amount on the day they are signed, so a rancher knows what he is being paid before committing to deliver [S3].

Forward contracts would have to be offered through open public bidding, with more than one bid solicited and bids made and accepted in view of buyers and sellers, instead of private one-on-one deals [S3].

Formula pricing — where the final price is calculated later from an index the seller cannot see — would be prohibited, with narrow carve-outs for futures-market prices and verifiable quality adjustments outside the packer's control [S2] [S3].
No single forward contract could cover more than 40 cattle or 30 hogs, limiting how much livestock one deal can lock up [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Meatpacking companies would bear the cost: they could no longer buy cattle and hogs under opaque formula-priced contracts, would have to let sellers see and compete in bids, would have to agree on a fixed dollar price when the contract is signed, and could not lock in more than 40 head of cattle or 30 hogs in a single forward contract [S3]. The Agriculture Department would gain enforcement duties, a public cost [S2].

drawbacks.text: Formula-priced and captive-supply contracts are not one-sided by design: they can smooth price swings for producers too, and an outright ban on contracts over 40 cattle or 30 hogs would take away a marketing tool that larger ranches and hog operations use to manage risk, not just a tool packers use against them [S3].

Requiring open bidding and fixed base prices on every forward contract would add transaction costs and paperwork to livestock marketing, costs that would fall partly on the producers the bill is meant to help [S3].
The bill never attracted a single cosponsor from either party, which suggests even farm-state senators saw problems with the approach or prioritized other livestock-competition measures [S4].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For independent ranchers and hog farmers, the benefit is real: transparent pricing and visible competing bids directly address the complaint that packers use formula contracts to pay producers prices no one can verify or shop against. The cost falls on packers and, secondarily, on larger producers who would lose the convenience of big forward contracts and would absorb some new marketing friction. The bill was blunt — a flat size cap and a near-ban on formula pricing rather than a disclosure standard — so an honest supporter would concede it might have been refined in committee. But the larger imbalance it targeted, concentrated packer buying power set against thousands of individual sellers, is real and went unaddressed.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Agriculture Committee the day it was introduced, never got a hearing or a vote, and died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Enzi introduced the bill on March 15, 2002, and it was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry [S5].
The committee took no further action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — before the 107th Congress ended on January 3, 2003 [S5].
The bill's purpose was to require fixed base pricing and open public bidding on livestock forward contracts, ban formula pricing, and cap contract size at 40 cattle or 30 swine [S2] [S3].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Meatpacking companies are better off, because the limits on formula-priced and non-bidded forward contracts never became law and they kept the existing contracting practices for the rest of the Congress. Livestock producers gained nothing from the bill's failure.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Meatpacking companies and concentrated hog operators

for.name: Michael B. Enzi
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and spoke for it on the Senate floor

against.name: Tom Harkin
against.role: Chair, Senate Committee on Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and never scheduled it for consideration, a hearing, or a vote before the Congress ended

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken; the bill's only Senate backer was Republican Michael Enzi, and no member of either party signed on as a cosponsor.

industries.note: The bill would directly restrict how the largest meatpackers buy cattle and hogs: no formula pricing, mandatory open bidding, fixed base prices, and tight limits on contract size [S2] [S3]. Packers' savings from opaque, formula-priced contracts come at the expense of the ranchers and hog farmers who sell to them, so the industry's interest in this bill ran against producers.
